concepts.definition: A method that learns a list of pieces by merging, again and again, the two pieces that sit next to each other most often in the corpus.
concepts.example: In the small Turkish corpus the first merges are pairs such as e+r, r+o, o+t.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking BPE knows meaning; it only counts how often pieces sit next to each other.

concepts.definition: A step in which two pieces are turned into a single new piece and written in the list.
concepts.example: When o + t are merged, "ot" becomes a new piece.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking a merge adds a whole word to the vocabulary; it works step by step, pair by pair.

concepts.definition: The order in which the merges were learned; they are applied to new text in the same order.
concepts.example: b + ot is only possible after o + t has been done.
concepts.pitfall: Shuffling the list or applying it in reverse order; you get different and often broken pieces.

concepts.definition: How many times a pair sits next to each other in the corpus (taking word frequency into account).
concepts.example: If a word appears 3 times in the corpus and contains "ur" once, that word adds 3 to the pair's count.
concepts.pitfall: Looking at how many different forms a word has and forgetting how many times it appears.

concepts.definition: A word that never appears in the corpus; because the merges are no use for it, it is split into small pieces.
concepts.example: `kalemlik` (pencil case) does not appear in the robot corpus, so it is represented letter by letter or with very small pieces.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the model will give an error on a word it does not know; the tokeniser can split any text.

quiz.prompt: In a small corpus, the word "dur" appears 3 times and the word "durur" appears 2 times. The words have been split into letters. How many times in total is the pair where "u" and "r" sit next to each other counted in the corpus?
quiz.explanation: "dur" contains the (u, r) pair once: 3 appearances x 1 = 3. "durur" contains it twice (d-u-r-u-r): 2 appearances x 2 = 4. Total 3 + 4 = 7. Both how many times the word appears and how many pairs it contains go into the count.

The code goes from left to right: d stays as it is, at the first u r pair it writes ur and skips r with i++; the same happens at the second pair. The result is d ur ur. Without the skip, r would also be written separately (the third option).

options: The second piece of the merged pair is not skipped (i++ is missing)
The condition should use || instead of &&
pop should be used instead of push
quiz.explanation: When the pair is merged, r has already gone into ur, but on the next round the loop reads r again and adds it separately. The fix is to write i++ in the merge branch. Starting empty is correct; with || even a single u would be merged.

quiz.prompt: What happens when the tokeniser meets the word "kalemlik", which never appears in the corpus?
options: It gives an error and stops
It splits the parts where the merges are no use into small pieces, into letters if needed
It replaces the word with the closest robot word
quiz.explanation: Learned merges only fit pairs that are common in the corpus. An unseen word has few of these pairs and breaks into small pieces; this way every text can still be represented. The word is not skipped or replaced with another word.

quiz.prompt: In the long run, how does BPE's rule of merging the common pair affect the pieces?
options: All words are split into pieces of equal length
Common words get close to a single token; rare words are split into more pieces
Only the longest words are merged
The pieces are chosen at random on every run
quiz.explanation: Because common pairs are merged first, common words become a single token within a few steps; the pairs of rare words are not seen often enough, so they stay in pieces. The algorithm is not random: the same corpus gives the same list every time.
